## Start by defining the quantity {#l1-define-the-variable }

A random variable assigns a **numerical value** to the outcome of a random experiment.

::: {.takeaway}
Let $X$ be the number of heads obtained when four coins are tossed.
:::

| Experiment outcome | Value of $X$ |
|:---|:---:|
| HHTT | 2 |
| HTHT | 2 |
| TTTT | 0 |

The rule stays the same: **count the heads**. Different outcomes can produce the **same value** of $X$.
<p class="booklet-cue">Booklet p. 35 · Complete the working in your booklet.</p>

::: notes
Connect this table to the applet: x represented one unchanged pen price in the algebra problem; X assigns a numerical head count to each possible random outcome. HHTT and HTHT are different outcomes with the same head count. The variable is the rule, not the outcome string or the most recent number alone. Random variables are conventionally named with capital letters; a lower-case letter can denote a particular observed value. The letter case itself does not make a variable random.
:::
